data.hook: Conservative supporters poured out their frustration after Senate Republicans let the SAVE America Act die, despite House passage and promises of tighter election rules.
data.name: Conservative Voters Feel Betrayed as Senate Blocks SAVE America Act
data.summary: The SAVE America Act aimed to require proof of U.S. citizenship for voter registration and photo ID at federal polls, passing the House multiple times but stalling in the Senate due to a lack of 60 votes amid Democratic opposition and no rule changes for a simple majority. Senate Majority Leader John Thune called the backlash from 'paid influencer world' and 'keyboard warriors' a political weapon that fueled fundraising and rifts ahead of elections, insisting the bill never had the numbers. Voters reacted with deep disappointment, accusing leaders of betrayal, vowing to abandon the party, and even sharing Declaration of Independence quotes on altering government, while some defended the Senate's stance on the impossible math.

data.hook: Voters handed Democrats control of the House and Senate with solid majorities. Yet the party's net favorability sits at -6 points, a far cry from past wave victories.
data.name: Democrats Win Big but Favorability Plunges to -6 After Midterms
data.summary: CNN analyst Harry Enten pointed out the sharp drop from +26 in 2006 and +3 in 2018, calling it a vote against Republicans rather than for Democrats. Despite flipping the Senate 56-44 and securing a wide House margin, frustration grew over retaining leaders like Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, whose approval ratings lag. Discussions highlight whether the party will tackle affordability issues or risk future backlash by sticking to the status quo.

data.hook: Democrats swept the 2026 midterms into congressional control, yet their net favorability sits at minus six points—a 'loveless landslide' as CNN's Harry Enten put it.
data.name: Democrats Win Midterms but Face Deep Public Skepticism
data.summary: A CNN analysis showed Democratic net favorability at -6 after the 2026 blue wave, far below +26 in 2006 and +3 in 2018, with RealClearPolling at 39% favorable versus 53% unfavorable. Enten noted low ratings for leaders like Hakeem Jeffries (-17) and Chuck Schumer (-30), even underwater among Democrats. A Pew poll of over 10,000 adults found 67% of Americans worried Democrats will over-focus on Trump investigations, versus 31% wanting more, signaling voters chose against Republicans more than for the party.

data.hook: Back in 1969, professors leaned modestly left at 39-33. Today, that balance tips at least 6-to-1 across many schools, with elite disciplines hitting even steeper ratios.
data.name: U.S. College Faculty Shifted Sharply Left Over Decades
data.summary: Historical surveys like the 1969 Carnegie Commission showed conservatives sometimes outnumbering liberals in STEM fields, but recent data reveals a stark change: ratios now reach 108-to-0 Democrats in some anthropology departments and 56-to-0 in communications. Charts from Eric Kaufmann and Mitchell Langbert's 2018 analysis highlight heavy liberal concentrations in humanities and social sciences, while engineering and business remain more balanced. Commenters debate causes, from 20th-century institutional capture to cultural shifts, questioning if intellect differences or historical contingencies explain the trend.

data.hook: A simple question on X—'Would you embrace Elon Musk as a DEM?'—drew raw, heated responses from users across the political spectrum.
data.name: Online Debate Erupts Over Embracing Elon Musk as Democrat
data.summary: User Sinfulskin sparked the discussion on November 21, prompting replies ranging from harsh rejections like 'I wouldn’t embrace that fucking Nazi if he were dead' to support for Sen. Bernie Sanders' call to curb billionaire election spending. Sanders had criticized Musk and others for pouring $2 billion into races, labeling it oligarchy, especially after Musk admitted feeling 'pretty foolish' about his $500 million backing of Republicans in the 2026 midterms that Democrats won. Defenders highlighted Musk's job-creating companies and pointed to Democratic donors like George Soros, revealing deep divides on campaign finance and billionaire political roles.

data.hook: Sen. Rick Scott called for the Senate to grind through holidays on judges and budget fixes, but supporters fired back with doubt over empty talk.
data.name: Conservative Backlash Grows Over Senate Holiday Break Plans
data.summary: After Republicans lost Senate control in the November midterms, Sen. Rick Scott urged staying in session past holidays to confirm judges, secure elections, balance the budget, and back the military. Critics dismissed it as rhetoric, pointing to John Thune's reelection as GOP leader and the Senate's planned breaks through December before Democrats take over on January 3, 2027. Frustrated voices labeled Republicans spineless and pushed graphics to vote out incumbents, highlighting a rift between leadership and the conservative base demanding real action in the lame-duck window.

data.hook: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pointed to groups inside America hell-bent on tearing down core values, starting right in K-12 classrooms captured by progressive indoctrination.
data.name: Hegseth Warns of Internal Threats and Cultural Suicide in Education
data.summary: In a widely shared video, Hegseth described America's greatest dangers as internal, driven by a loss of focus on foundational principles and an education system he called an indoctrination machine often fueled by foreign money. He stressed accountability as the key missing piece, with effects already showing in the Pentagon. Supporters called for action to protect the Republic, linking it to administration moves like state-led education reforms and school choice, while some posts question abolishing the federal Department of Education and cite shifting global demographics. Critics argue the views overlook other factors or lean partisan.

data.hook: In a closed-door meeting, Barack Obama looked at the new House Democratic freshmen and saw a true reflection of America — urging them to channel that diversity into real results.
data.name: Obama Advises House Democrats to Embrace Diversity and Avoid Complacency
data.summary: Former President Obama met with the incoming class of House Democratic freshmen in Washington, arranged by Hakeem Jeffries, to discuss generational change, ideological differences, and delivering for constituents. He praised the caucus's diversity, contrasting it with a 'golf country club' on the other side of the aisle during State of the Union addresses, and warned against complacency while encouraging bolder pushes on health care beyond the Affordable Care Act. The remarks drew praise from supporters as a nod to broad representation but sharp criticism from conservatives, who called them divisive and pointed to Obama's own country club memberships.

data.hook: Even after the midterms, a new poll reveals steady public support for tougher immigration enforcement, with sharp divides across party lines.
data.name: Poll Shows 51% of Americans Back Deporting Most Illegal Immigrants
data.summary: A fresh Economist/YouGov survey of 1,628 U.S. adults from November 13-16 found 51% favor deporting all or most people who entered illegally, including 23% wanting everyone gone immediately and 28% allowing exceptions for those married to Americans or long-term residents without records. Support splits sharply: 83% of Republicans back it, while 41% overall prefer limiting deportations to serious criminals and independents nearly even at 47% for broad action. The results challenge claims of shifting voter views and highlight ongoing debates over enforcement amid political promises like amnesty.

data.hook: A retired Navy mom and mother of three posted on November 19, 2026: 'I want there to be a civil war. There... I said it.' The simple statement pulled in over a million views and thousands of raw responses.
data.name: Retired Navy Mom's Civil War Wish Draws Heated Replies
data.summary: The @PoliticalStacy post, from a MAGA supporter, sparked some replies agreeing amid frustrations over issues like grooming scandals and political divides, with graphics calling to fight a supposed takeover. Critics, including a military analyst, warned of devastating costs—recalling the U.S. Civil War's 620,000 deaths, potentially 8-9 million today amid modern vulnerabilities like collapsed supply lines and neighbor betrayals. Many stressed focusing on elections and de-escalation over fantasies of tidy conflict, highlighting deepening polarization after the 2026 midterms.
